Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 6 periods = 240 minutes
Total: 6 periods · 4h 0min

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Read (pp. 125–128): read dialogue of Aarav, Ananya, Chachi aloud.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the dialogue by showing students the chapter's title and inviting them to share what they notice. Ask: 'What do you think Aarav and Ananya are looking at in the picture at the start of the chapter?' Accept a few quick responses.

Let us Read (pp. 125–128) — Teacher reads the full dialogue aloud with expression, assigning character voices for Aarav, Ananya, and Chachi. After the first read-through, the class joins in for a second read with students taking the three speaking roles.

Teacher pauses at key moments — when Chachi describes the fort's red stones, the Narmada River view, and the 13-feet tall statue — and asks students to visualise and share briefly what they picture in their minds.
Quick pair-share: each student tells their partner one thing Chachi said about Maheshwar that surprised or interested them most. Teacher listens in and takes brief stock of comprehension.

periods.teacher_notes: The dialogue is set in a warm family evening, which helps students connect emotionally before tackling the cultural details. Students often confuse Madhya Pradesh as a city rather than a state — gently clarify as the location comes up in the text. Keep the read-aloud unhurried so the Q-and-A rhythm between the children and Chachi registers clearly.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p. 128): answer four questions on Ahilya Bai, fort location, materials, and statue.

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites the class to recall the key people and places in the Maheshwar dialogue — Chachi, Aarav, Ananya, Queen Ahilya Bai, the Narmada River — building a quick word map on the board as students call them out.

Let us Think A (p. 128) — Teacher reads each question aloud: Who was Ahilya Bai? Where is Maheshwar Fort and what makes its location special? What materials were used? What does the statue represent? Students discuss in pairs, then share answers with the class; teacher guides and refines responses.

Students write their own answers to the four questions in their notebooks. Teacher circulates, prompting students who struggle with the statue question to re-read the last part of the dialogue where Chachi describes it admiringly.

Two or three volunteers read their answers aloud. Teacher highlights strong evidence-from-text choices and corrects any factual slips — for example, the distinction between the fort's red stones from Gujarat and Rajasthan and the fort's hillside location above the Narmada.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently conflate 'where the stones came from' with 'where the fort is' — the two are distinct and the dialogue makes both explicit. The answer about the statue works best when students link it to Chachi's admiring tone rather than treating it as a bare fact. A brief return to the relevant dialogue passage (pp. 127–128) helps students anchor their written answers in the text.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (p. 129): discuss what makes historical places interesting and personal fort preferences.
Let us Listen (p. 131): listen to passage on Maheshwari sarees; arrange four sentences in order.

homework.task_brief: Let us Speak A (p. 132): find out about a nearby historical place and prepare a short oral presentation.

time_bands.activity: Let us Think B (p. 129) — Teacher poses the first discussion question: 'What do you think makes historical places like Maheshwar Fort interesting?' Students share briefly in pairs before offering their ideas to the class. Teacher draws out reasons related to age, stories, craftsmanship, and famous people.

Second discussion question: 'If you were Aarav or Ananya, which part of the fort would excite you most — the overhanging balconies, the statue, or the temples? Why?' Students express and justify their personal choice; teacher encourages full-sentence answers referencing what Chachi said in the dialogue.

Let us Listen (p. 131) — Teacher reads the passage about Maheshwari sarees aloud at a steady pace three times. Students listen and then arrange the four given sentences (originally used pure silk → cotton introduced → reversible borders → national and international markets) in passage order in their notebooks.
Students share their sequenced answers; teacher confirms the correct order and briefly discusses why sarees evolved from pure silk to a silk-cotton blend, drawing on the passage.
Teacher introduces the homework task (Let us Speak A, p. 132): students are to find out about a historical place near their home from elders and be ready to share it orally in an upcoming sitting.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening task requires students to hold four sentences in working memory across three readings — pausing after each read to let students jot a keyword helps. Students often place the 'available nationally and internationally' sentence first because it sounds like a summary; the passage actually places it last. For the discussion questions, accept local-language words where students struggle but nudge toward complete English sentences.

periods.activity_title: Odd One Out, Silent 'g', and Word Meanings

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn A (p. 129): identify the odd word out from four sets of similar-meaning words.
Let us Learn B (p. 130): read aloud and underline words with a silent 'g' from a given list.
Let us Learn C (p. 130): match seven vocabulary words from the chapter to their meanings.

time_bands.activity: Let us Learn A (p. 129) — Teacher writes 'smiling, grinning, laughing' on the board and asks what these words share. Students say they all mean something happy. Teacher then presents the four sets (sad/unhappy/tearful/thrilled; talk/discuss/kind/speak; noisy/quiet/silent/calm; cotton/wooden/silk/woollen) and students circle the odd one out, explaining their reasoning aloud before writing.

Let us Learn B (p. 130) — Teacher writes 'design' and asks students to say it aloud, then asks: 'Which letter do you not hear?' Students identify the silent 'g'. Class reads each word from the given list aloud together (sign, light, goat, night, sing, sugar, king, high, magnet) and underlines the ones with a silent 'g', distinguishing them from words where 'g' is heard.

Let us Learn C (p. 130) — Teacher reads each word from the chapter (kindness, bravery, wisdom, majestic, unique, fierce, dedicated) and the class chorally repeats each one. Students then draw matching lines between the seven words and their meanings in Column B, working individually before comparing with a partner.

Quick review: teacher reads a meaning aloud ('being devoted to something') and asks students to call out the matching word. Repeat for two or three pairings. Teacher addresses any errors, particularly 'fierce' versus 'brave', which students often conflate.

periods.teacher_notes: The odd-one-out game works well when students are asked to explain their choice rather than simply circle — it reveals whether they understand the grouping principle. For the silent 'g' list, 'magnet' and 'sugar' often trip up students who expect the rule to apply uniformly; model each word's pronunciation clearly. The vocabulary in Let us Learn C all appears in Chachi's description of Queen Ahilya Bai, so brief contextual examples from the dialogue reinforce the meanings.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak B (p. 132): fill blanks with correct articles (a, an, the) in a short passage.
Let us Write A (p. 133): write a short description of visiting Maheshwar Fort — what you see and feel.

time_bands.activity: Let us Speak B (p. 132) — Teacher briefly reviews the three articles on the board with one example each (a fort, an elephant, the Narmada River). Students then work through the passage about the monkey on the oak tree, filling in each blank. Teacher circulates and notes common errors, especially 'a' versus 'an' before vowel sounds.

Whole-class check of the articles passage: teacher reads each sentence aloud and invites a student to supply the correct article, briefly explaining why. Pay special attention to 'an old man', 'an apple', 'an olive' where vowel-initial nouns require 'an'.

Let us Write A (p. 133) — Teacher models a short two-sentence opening on the board: 'I walk through the tall gateway of Maheshwar Fort and feel the cool stone under my hands. Above me, the overhanging balconies stretch out over the sparkling Narmada River.' Students plan their own description with three ideas (what they see, what they touch or hear, what they feel inside) before writing.

Students write their description independently. Teacher circulates to support students who are stuck, prompting with questions such as 'What does Chachi say the balconies look like? How does the view over the river make you feel?' Two volunteers share their sentences with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Articles and vowel-initial nouns reliably produce errors — 'a apple' and 'a olive' are the most common; keep the rule visible on the board throughout the word-work section. For the descriptive writing, students who have heard Chachi's enthusiastic descriptions of the fort in the dialogue will have rich material to draw on — encourage them to use the words from Let us Learn C (majestic, unique) in their descriptions. Finished pieces need not be more than four to five sentences; quality of sensory detail matters more than length.

periods.activity_title: Factual Paragraph Writing and Fort Jigsaw Craft

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write B (p. 133): write a short factual paragraph on Maheshwar Fort using lesson facts.
Let us Do (p. 134): make a fort jigsaw puzzle on cardboard, draw fort, cut and rearrange pieces.

time_bands.activity: Teacher builds a shared fact bank on the board by asking students to call out things they know about Maheshwar Fort from the dialogue — location, builder, materials, the river, the statue, Maheshwari sarees. Students copy five facts they want to use into their notebooks.

Let us Write B (p. 133) — Teacher models a topic sentence together with the class: 'Maheshwar Fort is a beautiful and historic fort in Madhya Pradesh, built by Queen Ahilya Bai.' Students then write their own short paragraph of three to five sentences using the fact bank, guided by teacher prompts: location first, then the building materials, then the person who built it, then something special about it.

Two or three students read their paragraphs aloud. Teacher gives brief formative feedback, highlighting strong factual detail and helping students refine sentences that mix up the fort's stones and their origin.

Let us Do (p. 134) — Each student draws a simple grid of puzzle-piece lines on thick paper or the back of a worksheet, draws a fort outline on the reverse side, cuts along the grid lines with scissors, and then mixes up the pieces and reassembles them. Students who finish early pair up and try solving each other's puzzle.

Quick share-out: teacher asks, 'What was the trickiest part of putting the fort puzzle back together?' Students respond briefly. Teacher links the craft back to the idea that historical monuments like Maheshwar Fort take enormous skill and care to build and preserve.

periods.teacher_notes: The factual paragraph is best written with the fact bank visible on the board so students do not have to hold too much in memory while composing. Remind students that a paragraph begins with a topic sentence and each following sentence adds one new fact. The jigsaw activity works with plain paper if cardboard is unavailable — the key experience is the drawing, cutting, and reassembling sequence that mirrors the craft traditions described in the chapter.

items.item_stem: In the conversation about Maheshwar Fort, Chachi tells Aarav and Ananya about the special stones used to build the fort. Where were these stones brought from?

what_each_option_reveals.C: May indicate the student is guessing a distant state without recalling Chachi's specific mention.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests the student has confused the stone origins with another northern-state association.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Indicates the student has not retained the geographical detail from Chachi's description.

items.item_stem: Chachi describes Queen Ahilya Bai as someone who ruled with kindness and wisdom. Using what Chachi says in the conversation, write two things Queen Ahilya Bai did for her people.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Queen Ahilya Bai built temples, schools, and wells for her people. She was a warrior queen who ruled with kindness and wisdom.

items.item_stem: Your teacher will read the passage about Maheshwari sarees aloud. Listen carefully. Which of the following correctly describes what happened FIRST in the history of Maheshwari sarees?

options.label: A
options.text: The sarees became available in international markets.

options.label: B
options.text: The sarees became famous for their reversible borders.

options.label: C
options.text: The weavers originally used pure silk.

options.label: D
options.text: Weavers used cotton yarn along with silk.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may be focusing on the passage's final statement rather than its opening.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has identified a later development in the passage and placed it first.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student recalls a key detail but misplaces it chronologically in the passage.
